title: Pellbrook Clinics: why are waits getting longer?
prompt: Pellbrook Clinics runs 8 private outpatient clinics in the English Midlands, where patients see senior specialist doctors (consultants). A year ago, a new patient waited about 2 weeks for a first appointment. Today the wait is about 6 weeks, and patients are starting to complain. The CEO has asked you to find out why waits have grown and how to bring them back down. How would you approach this?

facts.answer: Pellbrook runs 8 private outpatient clinics in the English Midlands. Consultants see patients in five specialties, mainly orthopaedics, dermatology, and ear, nose and throat. This case is about first appointments only; follow-up appointments run in separate sessions.
The CEO wants the average wait for a first appointment back to 2 weeks within 6 months, without opening new clinics or raising prices.

About 60% of patients are covered by two health insurers; the other 40% pay for themselves. A first appointment earns Pellbrook £200 either way. Both insurers have warned that they will start sending patients to other providers if waits stay above 3 weeks.

Consultants run 100 first-appointment sessions a week across the group, each with 10 slots. That has not changed in the last year. Consultants are paid a fixed £1,000 per session whether or not every slot is filled. Many say they would do extra Saturday sessions.

facts.question_topic: Rooms and costs of extra sessions
facts.answer: Rooms are not a constraint: the clinics are closed on Saturdays and about a quarter of weekday room time is unused. A Saturday session costs about £1,500 to run, including the consultant's higher Saturday rate and opening the building.

Requests for first appointments have been roughly flat over the last year, and the mix across specialties has barely changed. Marketing has not changed. Waits vary by specialty and clinic, from about 3 to 9 weeks; urgent referrals are fitted in within 2 weeks.

Patients book online or by phone and get one confirmation email. A year ago, to save money, Pellbrook stopped the reminder phone calls it used to make two days before each appointment. Cancelling or rebooking needs a phone call during office hours.

A slot is wasted when a patient does not turn up or cancels less than 48 hours ahead. These slots almost always stay empty, because Pellbrook has no list of patients who could come in at short notice. Patients who miss an appointment rarely rebook.

In a recent survey of patients who missed a first appointment, most said they had already been seen somewhere else while they waited, or no longer needed the appointment. A few said they had forgotten.

key_buckets: Demand: requests for first appointments and how they have changed
Capacity on paper: consultant sessions, slots per session and rooms
Capacity actually used: no-shows, late cancellations and empty slots
The booking process: reminders, cancelling and filling gaps at short notice
A plan to clear the backlog and keep waits down, with its cost and timing
good_signs: Treats the waiting list as a queue: waits grow when fewer patients are seen than ask for an appointment
Checks demand and capacity on paper before proposing new capacity
Asks how many slots are actually used, not just how many are offered
Separates two jobs: stop the list growing, then shrink the backlog
red_flags: Jumps to hiring consultants or opening clinics without checking how existing slots are used
Assumes demand must have risen without asking for the data
Ignores the link between long waits and missed appointments

exhibits.title: First appointments across the group in an average week
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask for demand and capacity for first appointments: requests, slots offered, how many slots are used and the size of the waiting list, now versus a year ago.
exhibits.insight: Requests and slots have not changed, but empty slots doubled from 100 to 200 a week (10% to 20% of slots). Pellbrook now sees 100 fewer patients a week than ask for an appointment, so the waiting list grew from 1,800 to 4,800: from 2 weeks to 6 weeks of patients seen.

exhibits.title: Empty slots last month, by how far ahead the appointment was booked (average week)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask which appointments end up empty, or whether missed appointments depend on how long the patient waited.
exhibits.insight: The longer a patient waits, the more likely the slot is wasted: 5% of slots booked under 2 weeks ahead are empty, against 25% of those booked more than 4 weeks ahead. Long-wait bookings cause 150 of the 200 empty slots (75%). Long waits create empty slots, and empty slots make waits longer: a vicious circle.

math.question: By how many patients a week is the waiting list growing now?
math.working: Slots used = 1,000 - 200 = 800 patients seen a week. 900 patients ask for an appointment, so the list grows by 900 - 800 = 100 patients a week.

math.question: Each first appointment earns £200. How much revenue a year do the empty slots cost Pellbrook, in £ million? Assume 50 working weeks a year.
math.working: 200 empty slots x £200 = £40,000 a week. Over 50 weeks that is £2,000,000, or £2 million a year. Consultants are paid per session anyway, so almost all of it is lost profit.

math.question: What percentage of empty slots comes from appointments booked more than 4 weeks ahead?
math.working: 150 of the 200 empty slots a week were booked more than 4 weeks ahead. 150 / 200 = 75%.

math.question: Suppose reminders and filling late gaps bring empty slots back to 100 a week, so Pellbrook again sees 900 patients a week, the same number as ask for one. It also runs Saturday clinics that see 250 extra patients a week from the waiting list. How many weeks until the list is down to a 2-week wait?
math.working: A 2-week wait at 900 patients a week means a list of 2 x 900 = 1,800. The list must shrink by 4,800 - 1,800 = 3,000. Weekday clinics now keep pace with requests, so only the Saturday clinics shrink the list: 3,000 / 250 = 12 weeks, about 3 months.

brainstorm.question: What could Pellbrook do to cut the number of empty slots, and to fill the ones that still come up?
idea_bank: Bring back reminders, for example a text a week before and two days before each appointment
Let patients cancel or rebook with one tap from the reminder, at any time of day
Keep a short-notice list of patients who can come in at a day's notice, and offer them freed-up slots
Contact everyone on the waiting list to check they still need an appointment, and remove those who do not
Book one or two extra patients into sessions where empty slots are common
Ask self-pay patients for a deposit, or charge a fee for late cancellations
Ask patients to confirm a week before, and release unconfirmed slots to the short-notice list
Run extra sessions to clear the backlog so that new bookings are only a few weeks ahead
Track empty slots by clinic and specialty every week and act on the worst

must_mention: Requests and slots are unchanged; the list grows because empty slots doubled from 100 to 200 a week, so 100 fewer patients are seen each week than ask for an appointment
Most empty slots (75%) are appointments booked more than 4 weeks ahead: long waits cause missed appointments, which make waits longer
A clear plan: cut empty slots with reminders, easy cancelling and short-notice filling, plus temporary Saturday clinics that clear the backlog in about 12 weeks, rather than new clinics
good_signs: Puts a value on the problem: empty slots cost about £2m of revenue a year
Checks that Saturday sessions pay for themselves: about £2,000 of fees against about £1,500 of cost per session
Suggests checking the waiting list, since many people on it may already have been seen elsewhere
Names what to track each week: the empty-slot rate, the size of the list and the wait, against the insurers' 3-week line

model_answer_outline: Clarify: first-appointment waits have gone from 2 to 6 weeks; the goal is 2 weeks within 6 months with no new clinics or price rises; both insurers will move patients if waits stay above 3 weeks.
Structure: treat the waiting list as a queue. Compare demand (requests) with capacity actually used (slots offered minus empty slots), then look at why slots go empty and how to clear the backlog.

Analysis: requests (900 a week) and slots (1,000) are unchanged, but empty slots doubled to 200, so only 800 patients are seen and the list grows by 100 a week. It has grown from 1,800 to 4,800, which is 6 weeks of patients seen.

Root cause: reminder calls stopped a year ago, cancelling is hard and freed slots are never refilled. 25% of slots booked over 4 weeks ahead go empty, against 5% of those booked under 2 weeks ahead, and they make up 75% of empty slots: the longer the wait, the worse it gets.
Maths: empty slots cost about £2m of revenue a year. If empty slots fall back to 100 a week and Saturday clinics see 250 extra patients a week, the list falls to a 2-week wait in 12 weeks.

Recommendation: restart reminders with one-tap cancelling, set up a short-notice list and check the waiting list now; run temporary Saturday clinics for about 3 months (each session earns more than it costs); tell the insurers the plan and track empty slots, the list and the wait every week.
